messages.body_plain:
Hello,

A huge thanks to Eric for responding to my questions. I am appending the solution that we agreed on. I shared a reproducible example along with test data for Eric to take a look at.

>From Eric:

There are a couple of changes I have made to your data/code:
rather than having each point as a stratum, I've reverted to having a single stratum sampled by 43 stations (change Region.Label)
you noted you visited each station 6 times; hence Effort should be 6 rather than 1
sometimes pairs of birds were detected rather than single individuals; ds() does not recognise the field "number" to indicate group size, so I change field name to "size" which is recognised by ds()
Fitting the hazard rate detection function model results in a single estimate for the stratum, rather than the station-specific estimates you desire.  The point-specific estimates are easily obtained recognising that station-specific detections divided by detection probability is the estimated number of birds at the station.

Those station-specific estimates are converted to densities as a result of dividing the estimated birds per station by the total area sampled (at the stratum level). Area sampled is
area of a circle for a station: pi * truncation distance^2 (you used 50 for truncation)
multiply this area by the number of visits (6)
multiply again by the number of stations (43)
pi*50^2*6*43 = 2,026,327 m^2 or 202.6327 ha
If you examine the component of the fitted model object trial$dht$individuals$bysample$Dhat - you will have those station-specific density estimates.

Thanks again Eric,
Vijay

messages.body_plain:
This issue is discussed in the following papers:
Howe, E.J., Buckland, S.T., Després-Einspenner, M.-L. and Kühl, H.S. 2017.  Distance sampling with camera traps.  Methods in Ecology and Evolution 8, 1558-1565.
Howe, E.J., Buckland, S.T., Després-Einspenner, M.-L. and Kühl, H.S. 2019.  Model selection with overdispersed distance sampling data.  Methods in Ecology and Evolution 10, 38-47.

CTDS requires that 'snapshot' moments are independent of animal locations.  That is not the case when cameras trigger when an animal is present.  If you try to use CTDS methods using just the initial triggering location of the animal, you will get abundance estimates that are way too high, as the snapshot moments only occur when an animal is present, and at the location where it entered the detection zone of the sensor.  (The latter distorts the distribution of distances from the point, biasing the estimated detection function.)  The reason for using lots of snapshot moments - in your case with 3s between each - is to ensure approximate independence between snapshots and animal locations.  (The method assumes a snapshot every 3s, although the only ones actually occurring were those when the video was running.)  Different approaches are possible if you want to use just the initial triggering event, but they make stronger assumptions, for example with respect to how animals move.

Steve Buckland

Good day Nilanjan,

Sorry for the delayed reply,
It's great that you programmed cameras to record long videos. That's ideal for CTDS because you can measure distances to animals at your predetermined snapshot moments, and any effect of trigger speed and recovery time on the data collected should be small (smaller than if you used bursts or short videos, such that cameras often stopped recording and triggered again while animals remained in the area monitored by the camera). 30-seconds videos will also ensure that some animals were detected while leaving the field of view at the sides. This ensures that theta is equal to the angle of view of the camera, even if the camera doesn't always trigger as soon as the animal enters the area of potential detection.

One likely cause of the difference between LTDS and CTDS estimates is responsive movement. Avoidance of researchers during LTDS surveys is a common concern, and causes negative bias. That's why people sometimes used LTDS surveys to dung piles for ungulates. Surveys of sign require estimates of creation and decay rates or initial marking of signs, but at least pellets don't move away as surveyors approach. Reactions to cameras can also cause bias in CTDS estimates. I suggest reviewing a subset of videos for each species to look for reactive behaviour. If animals react to cameras by approaching them (to short distances), or by standing in the field of view inspecting the camera (contributing more observations) then CTDS estimates would be positively biased. We recommend censoring observations of reacting animals beginning after they change their movement behaviour in response to cameras. Houa et al. (link below) describe a repeatable method for identifying and correcting for reactions to cameras in CTDS surveys.

https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.13510

Warm regards,
Eric Howe

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

About 10 years ago, when I first came to distance sampling and learned to use the mrds R package to fit detection functions, I learned that it was not possible to incorporate adjustment terms into a detection function that included covariates. Thomas et al. (2010) contained the statement "As with the MCDS engine, covariates can be incorporated into the detection function model; however, inclusion
of adjustment functions is not supported at present." And tutorials such as this one <https://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-covariates/covariates-distill.html> from Eric in March 2022 continued to confirm this with statements like "Note that covariates are not allowed if a uniform key function is chosen and if covariate terms are included, adjustment terms are not allowed."

Hi Jason,

I think experts' opinion varies on this.

My opinion is that there *can* be advantages to trying adjustment terms
in addition to covariates.  There is no strong reason to suppose that
the "true" detection function has a particular key function shape, so
including covariates allows more flexibility that means we are more
likely to get a good fit to the data and makes it more likely that
pooling robustness will operate and we will get low/no bias due to
unknown factors causing heterogeneity in the detection function.

However, one major difficulty with including adjustments with covariate
models is that we no longer have a viable mechanism to constrain the
fitted function to be monotonic nonincreasing (it is not feasible in
general to operate this constraint at every level of a continuous
covariate).  Also, trying lots and lots of models can lead to spurious fits.

On balance, I'd use adjustment terms with a lot of caution, perhaps only
in cases where a covariate model with either half normal or hazard rate
keys has a poor goodness-of-fit or other issues evident during model
checking. This seems congruent with what you say.  I'll be interested to
hear perspectives from others.

I did program up an R function recently to implement model selection for
key + adjustments + covariates for a visual shipboard line transect
survey of cetaceans, but ended up switching off the adjustment part when
covariates were in the model because I found the AIC-best models fit the
data fine without them except for the cases where there was some other
problem such as bow riding that requires a bespoke solution.  I'm happy
to share the code however if you drop me a line.

Regarding the monotonic nonincreasing issue, an alternative flexible
framework for detection functions is mixtures of monotonic nonincreasing
key functions.  Dave Miller and I published on this a decade ago
(https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0118726), but the models are
parameter-heavy and there is no maintained software to implement them
nor any current software that adds covariates.  Would be relatively easy
to program up however, and a fun research project.

Cheers, Len

messages.subject_clean: Gamma function instead of left truncation for a single-team line transect survey?
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am working with a single-team aerial line transect survey for marine mammals. The survey was flown in a Partenavia P68 with bubble windows, 1000 ft altitude (305 m), 100 kts ground speed (185 kph), and one observer on each side of the plane. There were approximately 500 sightings of large whales, the focal taxon in this case. Distances were estimated with clinometers except in a couple of sightings when wing strut marks were used. A histogram of inclination angles shows some heaping at 10 and 5 degree increments (see attached plot_DistanceMethod_by_Inclination.png), but the heaping is not extreme so I do not intend to conduct a binned analysis.

Histograms of perpendicular distances show a decline in sightings approaching distance 0 (see attached plot_DistanceMethod_by_Distance files). A traditional solution to this problem is to apply left truncation. In this example, the histograms suggest 100 m might be an appropriate left truncation distance. I do not have any other information that would help select a specific distance (e.g. controlled experiments of visibility conducted by this team). My current understanding is that the bubble windows afforded an adequate view of the transect line and the observers endeavored to monitor it carefully.

Recently, someone mentioned the idea of using a gamma key function rather than applying left truncation. The idea would be to directly model the decline in detections approaching the trackline, and thereby not have to discard any of the sightings, as would occur with left truncation. Is that a reasonable thing to do with a single-team survey, e.g. a CDS analysis?

I noted that Becker and Quang (2009, JABES) used a gamma-shaped detection function to model detectability of bears observed by aircraft in Alaska, and explained that "animals close to the transect appear to pass by so quickly that they are more difficult to observe than animals at moderate distances." Their survey was only at 100 m altitude while ours was at 305 m, but their speed was only 100-150 kph while ours was 185 kph. Anyway, it seems plausible that a similar effect could have happened on our whale survey. However, I'm not sure how using a gamma function relates to the g(0)=1 assumption of CDS/MCDS detection functions. Becker and Quang used a two-team approach. I have not studied their math in detail, but it appears this allowed them to scale the height of their gamma function appropriately while having g(0)=0, which seems to me to be the crux of fitting a gamma function properly given that some animals at x=0 may be missed for reasons other than the "passing quickly by" problem.

The data I'm working with only had a single team. Our current plan for addressing perception bias is to apply a correction factor estimated by a different survey program that was conducted in the same time and region but that used two teams and estimated a correction with MRDS. This is not perfect, but it is likely to be less biased than doing nothing.

Given that plan, is it then valid to try a gamma key function here with a CDS or MCDS analysis? Or should I stick to left truncation?

Assuming a gamma function is not valid with my CDS analysis, if this had been a two team survey that was tractable under MRDS, would a gamma function be appropriate then (using the mrds R package)? Would that essentially recreate the kind of analysis done by Becker and Quang?

Thanks for any advice you can suggest,

Jason

Arnaud

It took some "code archaeology" to deduce whether the MRDS code allowed adjustment terms  to be included with the gamma key function. The answer is "yes". I know of no published work where such a model has been implemented.

Below is code using the  golftee data supplied with the MRDS package demonstrating fitting such a model

library(mrds)
data(book.tee.data)
region <- book.tee.data$book.tee.region
egdata <- book.tee.data$book.tee.dataframe
#  eliminate detections at small distances
reduced <- egdata[egdata$distance>0.3, ]
samples <- book.tee.data$book.tee.samples
obs <- book.tee.data$book.tee.obs
# result <- ddf(dsmodel = ~mcds(key = "gamma", adj.series="cos", adj.order=1, formula = ~1),
#               data = egdata[egdata$observer==1, ], method = "ds",
#               meta.data = list(width = 4))
result <- ddf(dsmodel = ~mcds(key = "gamma", adj.series="cos", adj.order=1, formula = ~1),
              data = reduced[reduced$observer==1, ], method = "ds",
              meta.data = list(width = 4))
summary(result)
plot(result, main="Gamma with one cos adj")

> > > Hi everyone,
> > >
> > > About 10 years ago, when I first came to distance sampling and learned to use the mrds R package to fit detection functions, I learned that it was not possible to incorporate adjustment terms into a detection function that included covariates. Thomas et al. (2010) contained the statement "As with the MCDS engine, covariates can be incorporated into the detection function model; however, inclusion
> > > of adjustment functions is not supported at present." And tutorials such as  this one <https://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-covariates/covariates-distill.html> from Eric in March 2022 continued to confirm this with statements like "Note that covariates are not allowed if a uniform key function is chosen and if covariate terms are included, adjustment terms are not allowed."
> > >
> > > Has that changed, and is it now possible to include adjustment terms in detection functions that include covariates (i.e. MCDS detection functions)? Or was I wrong about this all along?
> > >
> > > If it is possible, is there any specific advice on the practice of including both covariates and adjustment terms in the same detection function? Certainly, with modern multi-core computers and R's convenient parallel processing libraries, it is almost trivial to craft code that can try large combinations of key functions and covariates, and an inclined user could trivially add a selection of adjustment terms and only multiply the number of combinations by perhaps 5 or 10.
> > >
> > > For my part, I am always nervous about adjustment terms, as they seem best used as proxies for parts of the detection process that either you don't understand or haven't collected covariates for. When you have a covariate, you can examine the detection function and consider whether the fitted relationship makes sense. When you use an adjustment term, it seems all you can say is "that fits the data better" (or not).
> > >
> > > Given my lack of deep knowledge about the statistical framework of MCDS and the detection function optimizer, I would be nervous about applying adjustment terms and covariates at the same time without an exceptional reason that was specific to the dataset under analysis. I'm just not sure how the two together would be handled mathematically. But I anticipate colleagues arguing we should take full advantage of our modern computing power to search by AIC for the best possible detection function we can, so let's add adjustment terms as "another dimension" to the combinations we search. It would be great to hear from the experts if they do or don't recommend that kind of practice.
> > >
> > > Thanks for your time and any advice you can provide. If there are specific manuscripts or books that discuss this, please let me know. Also I'm very interested in any examples in the literature that used both covariates and adjustment terms in the same detection model.
> > >
> > > All the best,
> > >
> > > Jason

Thank you Steve and Eric. Here's what I got applying gamma to these data.

First, regarding whether the histograms show the count of detections decreasing to zero as distance approaches zero. The attached plot_DistanceMethod_by_Inclination shows that the counts of detections approaches zero as inclination angle approaches zero. This is somewhat expected, because as inclination approaches zero, so does the change in perpendicular distance for a unit change in inclination. I guess the question is whether the counts of small inclinations are fewer than expected. The attached plot_DistanceMethod_by_Distance_50m_bins shows that sighting counts start dropping between perhaps 100-250 m perpendicular distance, depending on how you interpret it. So I think it could be argued that there is really a fall in detection counts all the way to zero for these data.

The attached Results.png shows summary statistics for various CDS models, ordered by AIC. gamma scores the best by AIC and Cramér–von Mises, and has the second-lowest CV. I also attached plots of the top three as well as the summary outputs.

gamma likely ranked best here because it fit the drop-off in detections better than the others. If I had left truncated, they would have outperformed it, of course.

If you have any more thoughts after seeing these results, I'm very interested to hear them. I will need to think more on the perception bias correction issue.

Thanks again,

Jason

> >

> >

Anyway, it seems plausible that a similar effect could have happened on our whale survey. However, I'm not sure how using a gamma function relates to the g(0)=1 assumption of CDS/MCDS detection functions. Becker and Quang used a two-team approach. I have not studied their math in detail, but it appears this allowed them to scale the height of their gamma function appropriately while having g(0)=0, which seems to me to be the crux of fitting a gamma function properly given that some animals at x=0 may be missed for reasons other than the "passing quickly by" problem.
> >

Our current plan for addressing perception bias is to apply a correction factor estimated by a different survey program that was conducted in the same time and region but that used two teams and estimated a correction with MRDS. This is not perfect, but it is likely to be less biased than doing nothing.
> >

> >
> > Assuming a gamma function is not valid with my CDS analysis, if this had been a two team survey that was tractable under MRDS, would a gamma function be appropriate then (using the mrds R package)? Would that essentially recreate the kind of analysis done by Becker and Quang?

> >
> > Jason

Nothing radical to say, just a couple of comments. If I was performing the analysis, I likely would have performed right truncation at ~3km before model fitting; that may have negated the need for an adjustment term for the half-normal key.

Right truncation aside, note that the two top models in your candidate set produce equivalent estimates of detection probability (almost) to the third decimal place. Hence, you density estimates would be virtually identical whichever model you chose as the basis for inference.

First, regarding whether the histograms show the count of detections decreasing to zero as distance approaches zero. The attached plot_DistanceMethod_by_Inclination shows that the counts of detections approaches zero as inclination angle approaches zero. I guess the question is whether the counts of small inclinations are fewer than expected. So I think it could be argued that there is really a fall in detection counts all the way to zero for these data.

The attached Results.png shows summary statistics for various CDS models, ordered by AIC. gamma scores the best by AIC and Cramér–von Mises, and has the second-lowest CV. I also attached plots of the top three as well as the summary outputs.

gamma likely ranked best here because it fit the drop-off in detections better than the others. If I had left truncated, they would have outperformed it, of course.

Jason

Thanks Eric and Steve, I'm glad you thought the gamma was reasonable.

Eric, I see what you mean about truncating at 3 km. If I was just estimating abundance with a traditional design-based survey, I'd probably go for that. I doubt the loss of a few more percent of sightings would affect things much, and maybe the tighter fit would yield a more precise estimate. But because this function is ultimately going to be used as part of a density surface model, I am loathe to give up more sightings than I need to, so that as many as possible will be available for the spatial modeling stage. I think the gamma looks pretty good going out to 5 km.

This function actually pools five different species, two of which are uncommon in the area. All five have similar detectability overall, but I'm planning to address any differences by including the species ID as a covariate. I'm also interested to see if this pooling allows other covariates to be selected, by virtue of having more data to work with, than might occur with five species-specific detection functions with fewer sightings in each.

Jason

Jason

It was all going so well ... until ...

You raised the subject of "covariate". See the toy example below:

library(mrds)
data(book.tee.data)
region <- book.tee.data$book.tee.region
egdata <- book.tee.data$book.tee.dataframe
#  reduce detections at small distances
reduced <- egdata[egdata$distance>0.3, ]
samples <- book.tee.data$book.tee.samples
obs <- book.tee.data$book.tee.obs
result <- ddf(dsmodel = ~mcds(key = "gamma", adj.series="cos", adj.order=1,  formula = ~sex),
              data = reduced[reduced$observer==1, ], method = "ds",
              meta.data = list(width = 4))
summary(result)
plot(result, main="Gamma with sex as covariate")

Thanks Eric and Steve, I'm glad you thought the gamma was reasonable.

Eric, I see what you mean about truncating at 3 km. If I was just estimating abundance with a traditional design-based survey, I'd probably go for that. I doubt the loss of a few more percent of sightings would affect things much, and maybe the tighter fit would yield a more precise estimate. But because this function is ultimately going to be used as part of a density surface model, I am loathe to give up more sightings than I need to, so that as many as possible will be available for the spatial modeling stage. I think the gamma looks pretty good going out to 5 km.

This function actually pools five different species, two of which are uncommon in the area. All five have similar detectability overall, but I'm planning to address any differences by including the species ID as a covariate. I'm also interested to see if this pooling allows other covariates to be selected, by virtue of having more data to work with, than might occur with five species-specific detection functions with fewer sightings in each.

Jason

Krista

Thanks for your interest in the distance sampling workshop; I presume you are interested in the next offering, taking place 05-16 May.

I'll be teaching that workshop and understand your hesitance about the workshop and the expectation about experience with R.  I hope to put you at ease when I say the emphasis of the workshop is learning about distance sampling. We use R to help learn about distance sampling; but R takes a back seat to distance sampling.

In the exercises, I provide you with all the code you need to complete the exercises; again the emphasis is upon understanding the results produced by the code you generate, rather than building the code itself. The workshop uses a cloud-based version of RStudio, avoiding the need to install R and RStudio and we begin quickly to analyse distance sampling data. Of course, after the workshop you will want to install R and RStudio on your own computer, but that is not a prerequisite for the workshop.

To answer you question specifically—where can you gain some experience with R ahead of the workshop, here are a couple of suggestions. A group of R users in Sydney have developed some materials, you might spend some time with their resources

https://rladiessydney.org/courses/ryouwithme/

particularly Lesson 3 (Lessons 1 and 2 are about installation, which as I noted above you can skip).

Have a look at that resource and if you have more questions, send me a note.

Eric Rexstad

Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling

University of St Andrews

Registered Charity in Scotland SC013532

Fiama

Welcome to the list. You are being very conscientious thinking about truncation and its effect upon segment area.

Recognise that the small number of detections will have at least two consequences: a) your estimate of detection probability will be compromised because the detection function model fitting will be speculative and b) the number of segments containing detections will also be small also compromising the predictive ability of the model-based inference regarding predictors influencing guanacos.

Those two challenges overshadow the challenge associated with enlarged segment sizes. Guidance about segment size is just that, guidance. Have a look at the following, where authors examined differing segment sizes and the effect of those sizes upon their inference
Redfern JV, Barlow J, Ballance LT, Gerrodette T, Becker EA (2008) Absence of scale dependence in dolphin–habitat models for the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean. Mar Ecol Prog Ser 363:1-14.  https://doi.org/10.3354/meps07495

One of their conclusions was
> The product-moment correlation coefficients between densities predicted at the different resolutions were quite high (Table 4), with average values ranging from 0.77 (Risso’s dolphin) to 0.92 (striped dolphin).
That conclusion won't necessarily hold for your system, but it is one of the few empirical examples where the question of segment size was investigated.

I would like to run code similar this: https://distancesampling.org/Distance/articles/web-only/CTDS/camera-distill.html, but where the sample fraction in the call to dht2 is a data.frame with 2 columns -- Sample.Label and fraction (because my fractions are different for each transect). I am trying to use this for Camera Trap Distance Sampling, where I would like to use multiple types of cameras, each with a different angle of view. See below for the exact code I ran. When I tried to run the call to dht2, R Studio crashed. I am running Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-10310U CPU @ 1.70GHz, 2208 Mhz, 4 Core(s), 8 Logical Processor(s), with Installed Physical Memory (RAM) 16.0 GB, Total Physical Memory 15.7 GB, Available Physical Memory 4.42 GB, Total Virtual Memory 18.1 GB, Available Virtual Memory 3.48 GB, and Page File Space 2.38 GB. I am assuming the reason for the crash is that the task was too computationally intensive for my computer, but I would like to hear what others think -- whether there's a way I can adjust the code to get around the limitations of my computer.

```# Code mostly copied from: https://distancesampling.org/Distance/articles/web-only/CTDS/camera-distill.html

# Data Input
trigger.events <- read.table(file="VideoStartTimes_FullDays.txt", header=TRUE)

trigger.events$date <- paste("2014",
                             sprintf("%02i", trigger.events$month),
                             sprintf("%02i", trigger.events$day),
                             sep="/")
trigger.events$time <- paste(sprintf("%02i", trigger.events$hour),
                             sprintf("%02i", trigger.events$minute),
                             sep=":")
trigger.events$datetime <- paste(trigger.events$date, trigger.events$time)

# Functions in the Activity Package
library(activity)
trigger.events$rtime <- gettime(trigger.events$datetime,
                                tryFormats = "%Y/%m/%d %H:%M",
                                scale = "radian")

act_result <- fitact(trigger.events$rtime, sample="data", reps=100)

# Adjustment for Temporal Availability
camera.operation.per.day <- 11.5
prop.camera.time <- camera.operation.per.day / 24
avail <- list(creation=data.frame(rate = act_result@act[1]/prop.camera.time,
                                  SE   = act_result@act[2]/prop.camera.time))

### DETECTION DATA ANALYSIS ###

DuikerCameraTraps <- read.csv(file="DaytimeDistances.txt", header=TRUE, sep="\t")
DuikerCameraTraps$Area <- DuikerCameraTraps$Area / (1000*1000)
DuikerCameraTraps$object <- NA
DuikerCameraTraps$object[!is.na <http://is.na>(DuikerCameraTraps$distance)] <- 1:sum(!is.na <http://is.na>(DuikerCameraTraps$distance))

# Distance Recording
breakpoints <- c(seq(0, 8, 1), 10, 12, 15, 21)
hist(DuikerCameraTraps$distance, breaks=breakpoints, main="Peak activity data set",
     xlab="Radial distance (m)")

# Detection Function Fits
library(Distance)
trunc.list <- list(left = 2, right = 15)
mybreaks <- c(seq(2, 8, 1), 10, 12, 15)
conversion <- convert_units("meter", NULL, "square kilometer")
uni3 <- ds(DuikerCameraTraps, transect = "point", key = "unif", adjustment = "cos",
           nadj = 3, convert_units = conversion,
           cutpoints = mybreaks, truncation = trunc.list)

viewangle <- 42 # degrees
samfrac <- viewangle / 360
peak.uni.dens <- dht2(uni3, flatfile=DuikerCameraTraps, strat_formula = ~1,
                     sample_fraction = samfrac, er_est = "P2", multipliers = avail,
                     convert_units = conversion)
print(peak.uni.dens, report="density")

# My adjusted code (this causes R studio to crash)
# Based on pg. 18 of https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/Distance/Distance.pdf
# where it says this regarding the sample fraction term of the model: proportion
# of the transect covered (e.g., 0.5 for one-sided line transects). May be specified
# as either a single number or a data.frame with 2 columns Sample.Label and fraction
# (if fractions are different for each transect)

# Created that 2-column data.frame to test this out
samfrac_variable <- data.frame(
  Sample.Label = DuikerCameraTraps$Sample.Label,
  fraction = DuikerCameraTraps$multiplier)
samfrac_variable <- edit(samfrac_variable) # In this step I edited ~ 30 of the
# values to be slightly smaller than the others, to mimic what I might be working
# with in my study

peak.uni.dens <- dht2(uni3, flatfile=DuikerCameraTraps, strat_formula = ~1,
                      sample_fraction = samfrac_variable, er_est = "P2", multipliers = avail,
                      convert_units = conversion)
print(peak.uni.dens, report="density")```

  Sample.Label = unique(DuikerCameraTraps$Sample.Label),

                   min=DuikerCameraTraps$multiplier, max=0.3))

library(remotes)
